# Methods (DRAFT; generated by tools/methods.py from the data files, do not edit by hand)

Run profile: full (5,000 Monte Carlo draws). Draft text of the methods and their results, in five parts generated from the data files (the deterministic numbers do not depend on the profile). Every figure: FIGURES.md; every output file: INDEX.md. References: docs/REFERENCES.md.

## Contents

* 1. Baseline projection
* 2. Planetary-boundary layer (AESA)
* 3. Pathways and the theoretical limit
* 4. Attribution principle, release accounting, replacement and the history
* 5. Uncertainty analysis

## 1. Baseline projection

Every result below is read from the run outputs (outputs/data/; settings from projection.py). Adopted run: Reference (net replacement half-life 10 yr); 2026 overbuild rule `market_excess`.

### Data freeze and scope

Data freeze: building consents to September 2026 (Stats NZ BLD468601); population estimates to the June 2026 quarter (Stats NZ estimated resident population); household projections 2023-base (Stats NZ National family and household projections, released 11 November 2026). Later releases are not used.

Scope: the model covers new dwellings. Consents to alter existing dwellings (no floor area published) are outside scope, about 12% of residential consent value in 2025 (Stats NZ BLD468601, 2025). Both budgets use the same new-build scope (the acquired-rights base from the new-build history; the ability-to-pay share from new-build consent value), so the exclusion is consistent.

### Summary

New Zealand is projected to build 105.4 million m² of new residential floor area in 2026–2050 in the Reference. In 2026–2050 this emits 25.5 Mt CO₂e: 25.1 Mt from materials and construction (A1–A5) and soil carbon loss, counted in the construction year, and 438 kt of maintenance (B2, B4), 2026–2050. A further 9.7–10.7 Mt is committed after 2050 (later B2/B4 and C1–C4; outputs/reports/reconciliation.md). How fast existing dwellings are replaced is the largest structural uncertainty: Low replacement (the long-run rate throughout) gives 101.2 million m², High replacement (the 2018–2023 rate persisting) 110.9 million m², and Very High replacement (trend continues) (the weighted linear trend of the census-interval rates 1991–2023 continues) 116.7 million m². Within the Reference, joint uncertainty in the inputs gives a 90% interval of 88.5–124.9 million m² (median 105.4, mean 106.0). Outside the Monte Carlo, carbon-factor and soil bounds on the Reference carbon (25,503 kt): case-study jackknife 24,627–26,320 kt, single case study 20,160–30,453 kt, soil order 23,336–34,677 kt. Population uncertainty alone (Stats NZ 5th–95th percentiles) spans 91.1–122.0 million m². The joint interval is narrower than the population-only range because each population draw also moves household size along the matching Stats NZ Low/High variant: low-population variants come with smaller households (an older age structure), so the number of households varies less than population, whereas the population-only range holds household size on the Medium shape.

#### The 2026 overbuild rule

Building in the pipeline years 2026, 2027 is observed, not modelled: completions = 0.945 x consents lagged 17 months (consents observed to 2026–09–01): 2026 32,016 dwellings, +6,225 above the requirement; 2027 38,658 dwellings, +5,664 above the requirement. From 2028 building stays above the requirement by gap_ref x rho^(t-2027), with gap_ref = building 2027 - requirement 2028 = +5,013 and rho = 0.43 (the estimated persistence of departures from the calibrated identity). The 2026 overbuild is STOCK-ADDING: the extra dwellings join the stock as additional vacant dwellings, soil carbon loss applies (new footprints) and removals stay on the path of the replacement variant. The surplus is absorbed by 2035: the remaining surplus U(t) = C(t) (1 - w(t)), C the cumulative excess and w the normalised logistic (w = 0 up to the last observed year, w >= 2035 = 1), and the absorbed part is built less (payback, capped at the year's building, any shortfall carried). Market excess +15,728 and absorbed -34,694 dwellings over 2026–2050 (net -18,966), on top of whichever replacement variant runs. Stock-flow theory of the housing market (Rosen & Smith 1983; Wheaton 1990; DiPasquale & Wheaton 1992; Gabriel & Nothaft 2001) fixes the direction of the adjustment, the reversion of vacancy to its equilibrium rate, but not its speed: 2035 is the common RECC adoption window of the model and the speed is bracketed by sensitivity rows (never absorbed, by 2030, by 2045). Implied stock vacancy (1 - households / (stock + cumulative 2026 overbuild)) peaks at 6.72% in 2028 and is 5.39% in 2050, against 5.08–8.09% at the censuses 1986–2023 (pre-2013 values on the earlier empty definition).

The vacancy-rate parameter is held at its published 2023 census value (5.39%; on the consistent definition 2023 is the series maximum, 5.38%, minimum 4.01% in 1996); the starting surplus and the 2026 overbuild raise implied stock vacancy temporarily and are absorbed by 2035, so implied vacancy returns to the parameter (5.39% in 2050). In 2050 implied stock vacancy is -0.0 percentage point above the 2023 rate; never absorbed, floor area would be +4.5%.

Caveats: the absorption speed is not identified by the eight census vacancy observations; over 2018–2023 part of the excess building went to redevelopment and household formation instead. rho is estimated on the calibrated identity, not on market cycles. Sensitivities: booking as stock-neutral redevelopment (implied net removals then peak at 9,735 in 2026), absorption never, by 2030 or by 2045, and the gap measured against the 2026 requirement.

#### Soil method

Soil carbon loss is the loss of soil organic carbon when land is built on (land-use change): a new building footprint seals the soil under it, while a rebuilt footprint sits on soil already sealed. Soil carbon loss is therefore applied to all floor area except the Demolition replacement band (demolition, net of unconsented additions) and the Recent replacement surge band, where it is zero. The factor is 58.77 kg CO₂e per m² of footprint, the area-weighted average over the 10 soil orders of the land zoned for urbanisation to about 2050 in Auckland, divided by each typology's floor space index (Christoforatos, Pickering & Schipper 2026, Journal of Environmental Management 415, 130603, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.130603). The Raw and Organic soil-order extremes are the bounding sensitivity. Carbon factors for materials come from 16 New Zealand case studies (Christoforatos & Pickering 2025, Smart and Sustainable Built Environment, https://doi.org/10.1108/SASBE-06-2025-0304).

### Validation

Rolling-origin hindcast of dwellings built (actual households and vacancy fed in; the net-replacement term predicted). Vacancy on a consistent definition (the pooled 2018/2023 empty share, 49.2% of unoccupied, at every census; the 2013 census share was 76.2%, and published empty vacancy falls 8.09% -> 5.08% across the 2013->2018 definitional break); vacancy as published in the last column.

| origin | test years | long-run rate (Low replacement rule) error | Reference rule error | best alternative | Reference rule, vacancy as published |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2006 | 2007–2023 | -3.9% | -4.2% | constant +1.0% | -14.9% |
| 2013 | 2014–2023 | +5.4% | +10.6% | constant +7.7% | -6.8% |
| 2018 | 2019–2023 | -10.5% | -11.4% | linked +2.9% | -11.3% |

Under a consistent vacancy definition the Reference rule reproduces building from the 2006 and 2013 origins to 2023 within 4–11%; the residual miss (-11.4% from 2018) is the 2018–23 surge.

Out-of-sample check (model run without 2026 data; completion lag 17 months): 2027 building observed in the pipeline 38,658 dwellings vs model 31,874; ratio 1.21.
Decomposition of the 2026 gap in the Reference (consents lagged 17 months): +16 dwellings = population -6,209 + pipeline from 2025 +6,225 + 2026 consents above requirement +0.

### Finding: 2026 building runs well above the model's requirement

With the 17-month completion lag, 2026 completions come from consents issued before 2026: observed 2026 building (consents lagged) is 32,016 dwellings against a Reference requirement of 32,000 (gap +16)[^low], all of it pipeline; 2027 pipeline building is 1.21 times what the Reference run without 2026 data implies. Population does not explain it: population growth over the year to June 2026 fell short of the projection, which lowers the requirement by 6,209. The gap is building already in the pipeline from 2025 (+6,225) plus 2026 consents above requirement (+0). Over 2018–2023 most building above household formation went to redevelopment (net removals 16,770) rather than vacancy (+6,286).

The model takes 2026 building from the observed consents and carries the excess forward as the 2026 overbuild (+6,225 dwellings in 2026, then gap_ref +5,013 fading at rho = 0.43; market excess +15,728 dwellings over 2026–2050, absorbed by 2035, net -18,966).

[^low]: In Low replacement (long-run rate) the requirement is 29,738 and the gap +2,278 = population -6,209 + pipeline +8,487 + 2026 consents above requirement +0.

### Planetary-boundary layer (AESA): climate change

Against the 2 °C carrying capacity (Bjørn & Hauschild 2015), allocated to the sector by acquired rights (AR; Horup et al. 2025) and ability to pay (AtP; Hjalsted et al. 2021), the boundary is 172.4 kt CO₂e (AR) and 43.35 kt (AtP) in 2026, and 182.5 / 45.87 kt in 2050 (AtP = 25.1% of AR in every year). Over 2026–2050 the Reference exceeds them 5.76-fold (AR; Monte Carlo p5-p95 5.00–6.62) and 22.9-fold (AtP; 19.6–26.6). The two principles are a range and are not averaged. Methods, constants, sources and limitations: the AESA section of outputs/reports/METHODS_DRAFT.md; settings: outputs/reports/ASSUMPTIONS.md. The emissions committed after 2050 (later B2/B4 and C1–C4) by the 2026–2050 cohorts (9,728–10,662 kt) equal 53–58 years of the 2050 AR boundary; they fall after 2050 and are not part of the cumulative LoE 2026–2050.

| JUDGEMENT | 2026 overbuild: stock-adding (vacant dwellings), fading at rho, absorbed by 2035 (logistic; theory fixes the direction, not the speed; never / 2030 / 2045 as sensitivities) |

| RULE | Starting surplus: the 2024–2025 building beyond the stock identity, if above the 1992–2023 census-interval mean + 2 SD, carried as vacant dwellings at the start of 2026 and absorbed with the overbuild by 2035 |
| JUDGEMENT | Completion lag: consents become completions 17 months later (monthly), at a completion rate of 0.945 |

### Open limitations and data needs

- No national demolition data: demolition of detached buildings up to three storeys is consent-exempt, so the implied replacement rates cannot be tested against a count.
- Household size is the Stats NZ 2023-base ratio of people in households to households, applied as a shape rebased on the observed 2023 household size of the total population: the share of the population outside private dwellings is held at its 2023 level.
- The living-arrangement propensities are held at 2023 (Stats NZ projection A); their change modelled on the 2001–2023 censuses (B) is a one-at-a-time row, not sampled in the Monte Carlo.
- Timber C1–C4 includes landfill methane (biogenic CO2 excluded), with decay as in the underlying EPD data: the 247 sawn-timber lines of the LCAQuick results carry C1–C4 of 1.1–4.5 times their A1–A3 (median 4.3), each with a module D credit for landfill-gas recovery. Timber is 31% of the case studies' C1–C4. No timber line carries a replacement or repaint event, so it affects the committed emissions after 2050, not the 2026–2050 total.
- Households 2019–2023: the Stats NZ Dwelling and household estimates remain on the 2018 Census base; Stats NZ has not yet rebased them on the 2023 Census. Their increments after the 2018 base are therefore rescaled by one factor (k = 0.824) so that June 2023 matches the 2023 census, as Stats NZ benchmarks each base; the consent-driven shape is kept. Both census endpoints are fixed, so only the timing of household growth within 2019–2023 depends on the rescaling. Stats NZ's 2023-rebased household estimates will replace it when published.
- With the typology mix held in every variant (internal to the model: it weights the case-study factors), neither the variants nor the Monte Carlo carry typology-mix uncertainty; a change of mix is a pathway question for later work, not a baseline uncertainty.
- The soil factor was derived for Auckland's future urban zones and is applied nationally.
- The case-study carbon factor for apartments rests on one independent case study (A_1 and A_2 are one design at two scales).
- The regional analysis of the recent replacement surge (replacement half-life by territorial authority) is deferred.
- Net replacement persistence (the replacement half-life of the Reference) is not identifiable from the census record; Low replacement and High replacement bound it.
- The 2018 census empty-dwelling count has no quality rating (DataInfo+); the vacancy terms rely on it.
- The 2026 overbuild fades at the persistence estimated on the calibrated stock identity (rho), not on market cycles (an assumption).
- Retirement-village floor area is reported but out of carbon scope.
- The vacancy-rate parameter is held at its published 2023 census value (5.39%; on the consistent definition 2023 is the series maximum, 5.38%, minimum 4.01% in 1996); the starting surplus and the 2026 overbuild raise implied stock vacancy temporarily and are absorbed by 2035, so implied vacancy returns to the parameter (5.39% in 2050). The 2026 overbuild (market excess ≈15,700 dwellings over 2026–2050, of which ≈14,100 in 2026–2028) is absorbed by 2035 along the normalised logistic of the levers (≈34,700 dwellings built less; implied vacancy peaks at 6.72% in 2028). Stock-flow theory of the housing market (Rosen & Smith 1983; Wheaton 1990; DiPasquale & Wheaton 1992; Gabriel & Nothaft 2001) fixes the direction, reversion of vacancy to its equilibrium rate, not the speed; 2035 is the common RECC adoption window of the model and the speed is bracketed by sensitivity rows (never absorbed, by 2030, by 2045). The persistence rho = 0.43 describes how the flow deviation fades, not the payback of the stock.
- Decarbonisation paths are relative changes for European and global market processes modelled with premise on ecoinvent 3.9.1 (Horup et al. 2025); they are applied as relative changes to New Zealand case-study factors. This assumes NZ material supply decarbonises at the same relative rate as those markets, which is not tested.
- Items without a counterpart in Horup et al. follow a labelled proxy path (polymers, paint and SIP at EPS, the smallest reduction in the set; gypsum plasterboard at clay brick) or are held at 2025 (the lift); the proxies are a judgement, bracketed by holding them at 2025 (sensitivity).
- C1–C4 (end of life) is held at 2025 factors (no source for end-of-life decarbonisation); future end-of-life technology would lower the committed emissions (conservative).
- Horup et al. (2025) SI Table S4 gives the average of the 9 premise scenarios only; the scenario range is shown graphically in their Fig. 2, so no low/high decarbonisation path is implemented.
- Several items are made in New Zealand with electricity-intensive production (aluminium, Pink Batts glass wool, Pacific Steel rebar, WPMA Radiata timber, Nelson Pine LVL); the aluminium items are stated in their EPD names to use mainly renewables-generated electricity. Where their 2025 factors already reflect low-carbon electricity, the premise paths, which include the decarbonisation of electricity supply ("The Premise software accounts for future changes in several critical sectors (supply of conventional and alternative fuels, electricity, cement and steel production and freight and passenger road transportation), and includes implementation of technologies such as carbon capture and storage in steel and cement production" (Horup et al. 2025, p. 5)), may overstate their relative reduction; a sensitivity holds them at 2025.
- Composite floor decking (an RC item containing its steel deck and rebar) follows the concrete-structure path because the source gives no split; this is conservative versus steel profile for the steel share.
- Event timing is deterministic (n events evenly spaced in the building life). Resch et al. (2021, Section 2.2 and Fig. 4) model replacement years as probability-distributed; the L / n sensitivity brackets the timing within the service-life range implied by the counts, but not early or late failures.
- A4–A5 follows a generic technological-progress factor (Resch et al. 2021, Table 1) because it cannot be separated by material process; Horup et al. (2025, Fig. 2A, pp. 5–6) show that generic factors oversimplify material-specific trends, and Resch et al. state that "the decay functions should not be interpreted as predictions" (p. 4). Sensitivities: held at 2025 and the item S4 paths.
- Emissions committed after 2050 (later B2/B4 and C1–C4) are a range bounded by two conventions (2025 factors; the 2050 factors held), not a projection: the source paths end in 2050 and C1–C4 has no decarbonisation source.
- The repaint composition differs from the first coat but cannot be separated in the source file; repaints take the line's initial stage split (negligible: the paint path is the EPS proxy).
- Completion rate 0.945 and its band 0.93–0.96 rest on Auckland consents (Greenaway-McGrevy & Jones 2023; Jones, Greenaway-McGrevy & Crow 2025), applied nationally; the upper milestone is published only as ">95%" (0.96 is a stated edge).
- The 17-month consent-to-completion lag is the midpoint of the Auckland median of 1.27–1.53 yr (Greenaway-McGrevy & Jones 2023; Jones, Greenaway-McGrevy & Crow 2025), applied nationally as one fixed lag (no distribution of build times).

### Figures

The figures of the paper: outputs/paper/PAPER.md; Extended Data: outputs/extended_data/EXTENDED_DATA.md; every other figure: outputs/diagnostics/DIAGNOSTICS.md. Where the projection leaves the 1991–2025 range: outputs/reports/reality_checks.md.

## 2. Planetary-boundary layer (AESA)

The planetary-boundary layer is an absolute environmental sustainability assessment (AESA) of New Zealand new residential construction, climate change only, 2026–2050. Static carrying capacity; two allocation principles reported as a range and never averaged. This layer does not change the model; it reads the model's outputs.

### Equations as implemented (aesa.py)

**Acquired rights** (Horup et al. 2025, Sci. Total Environ. 966, 178780, Eq. 1, p. 4):

    B_AR(t) = SOS · (Ī_sec,base / I_glob) · [P_NZ(t) / P_NZ(t0)] · [P_W(t0) / P_W(t)],   t0 = 2025

Ī_sec,base is the mean annual sector impact 2016–2025 from this model's own history (same scope, accounting rule and soil convention as the projection; at the case-study factors, roughly contemporaneous with the base window and not back-cast: past construction used past technology, so the decarbonisation of A1–A3 applies only to 2026–2050). Over the base window LoE_AR = I_glob / SOS = 8.1938 by construction (the sector impact cancels); the information is in the trajectory relative to the base.

**Ability to pay** (Hjalsted et al. 2021, J. Ind. Ecol. 25, 6–19, Table 2 Eqs. 5–6, p. 11; SI Eq. S1):

    SoSOS_ind(t) = SOS / P_W(t) · (g_W / g_NZ) · α
    B_AtP(t)     = SoSOS_ind(t) · P_NZ(t) · s_sec
    α            = 1 / Σ_c [(P_c / P_W) (g_W / g_c)]   (SI Eq. S1 with GDP totals, rewritten per capita)

g = GDP per capita in base year b = 2024, held fixed; g_W = Σ P_c g_c / Σ P_c and P_W = Σ P_c over the same covered economies. B_AtP / B_AR = (g_W/g_NZ) · α · s_sec · (P_NZ(t0)/P_W(t0)) · (I_glob/Ī_sec,base) is constant in this static design: 0.2514.

**Carbon factors.** A1–A3 of each case-study EPD item decarbonised 2026–2050 after Horup et al. (2025) SI Table S4 (item-level mapping, data/material_item_map.csv: direct, Horup p. 6, proxy or held), for construction and for the A1–A3 share of maintenance (B2, B4; replacement and repaint events); A4–A5 e^(-0.01 (t - 2025)) after Resch et al. (2021) Table 1; C1–C4, held items and soil carbon loss at 2025 (see outputs/reports/ASSUMPTIONS.md).

**Accounting.** Time-resolved: the sector impact I_sec(t) counts the materials and construction (A1–A5) and soil carbon loss of the construction in year t and the maintenance (B2, B4; replacement and repaint events) that occurs in year t in buildings built from 2026. Maintenance events after 2050 and all end-of-life emissions (C1–C4) of the 2026–2050 cohorts are committed after 2050, reported below as a range and in years of the 2050 AR boundary; they are not part of the cumulative LoE. On time-differentiated climate accounting of New Zealand building elements see McLaren et al. (2025).

**Level of exceedance**: LoE_k(t) = I_sec(t) / B_k(t); cumulative LoE = Σ I_sec / Σ B_k over 2026–2050 (ratio of sums).

**Dating.** Model year t is 31 December (Stats NZ ERP history). The WPP 2024 series (1 July) and, in the sensitivities, the Stats NZ (30 June) and WPP New Zealand series are dated at t as the mean of mid-year t and t+1.

s_sec uses the consented value of new residential building over national final consumption expenditure, following the FCE upscaling of Hjalsted et al. (2021) as a proxy of the priority households give to housing. In the national accounts residential construction is gross fixed capital formation, not final consumption; treating it as consumed follows the endogenisation of capital in consumption-based accounting (Södersten, Wood & Hertwich 2018).

Used as the global-impact sensitivity (EF31: the SOS of pair A, acquired rights only) |

Primary pair A: 2 °C carrying capacity (Bjørn & Hauschild 2015); sensitivity C: 1 W/m² planetary boundary (Bjørn & Hauschild 2015). Global-impact sensitivity (acquired rights only): I_glob = 7.55E+03 kg CO₂e per person x 6,895,889,018 persons (2010) = 5.206E+13 kg CO₂e/yr, the EF 3.1 normalisation factor (Andreasi Bassi et al. 2023, Table 10), with the SOS of pair A; AtP does not depend on I_glob.

### One-at-a-time rows and the AR base (shared-parameter rule)

A shared uncertain parameter is sampled once and used wherever it applies (Groen & Heijungs 2017; Kim, Mutel & Hellweg 2025): the present-day carbon factors enter both the acquired-rights base and the projection, so rows that change their level, or an accounting convention, recompute the base; rows that change only future technology or siting do not. The recomputed base uses the function of the Monte Carlo (boundaries.base_with_factors) at the row's own factors; the classification is boundaries.AR_BASE_RULE.

### Results

The 2 °C carrying capacity (Bjørn & Hauschild 2015) allocated by acquired rights gives 172.4 kt CO₂e in 2026 and 182.5 kt in 2050; by ability to pay 43.35 and 45.87 kt (25.1% of AR in every year). Both rise: New Zealand's share of world population grows between 2026 and 2050. Over 2026–2050 the Reference emits 25,503 kt against cumulative boundaries of 4,427 kt (AR) and 1,113 kt (AtP): cumulative LoE 5.76 (AR; Monte Carlo p5-p95 5.00–6.62) and 22.9 (AtP; 19.6–26.6).

### Limitations

- Static carrying capacity: the carrying capacities are constant yearly values modelled at steady state and their timespan may not match the assessment period (Clausen et al. 2025, pp. 143 and 148).
- Accounting (time-resolved): the sector impact of 2026–2050 counts materials and construction (A1–A5) and soil carbon loss in the construction year and maintenance (B2, B4) in the year it occurs. Maintenance after 2050 and all end-of-life emissions (C1–C4) of the 2026–2050 cohorts are committed after 2050, outside 2026–2050; they are reported as a range (outputs/data/aesa/results.json "committed", Fig3c) in years of the 2050 AR boundary and are not compared with the 2026–2050 boundary. Whole life at construction is a sensitivity.
- Carbon factors and the AR base: the case-study factors (BRANZ LCAQuick 3.6, built from EPD and BRANZ data) are roughly contemporaneous with the 2016–2025 base window, so the base uses them without back-casting; the vintages of the underlying EPDs are not tabulated. The base follows the projection's accounting rule (materials and construction and soil carbon loss of the base window's construction plus the maintenance within the base window of the cohorts built in it).
- The primary SOS (6.81E12) is the 2 °C carrying capacity of Bjørn & Hauschild (2015), not the 1 W/m² planetary boundary (3.61E12, sensitivity C). Sala et al. (2020, Table 3) label 6.81E12 as radiative forcing after Rockström et al. (2009), which does not match its derivation in Bjørn & Hauschild (2015).
- GWP basis: Bjørn & Hauschild (2015) ESM2 uses AR5 GWP100 factors (CH4 28, N2O 265; column "CFs (GWP100, IPCC5)") while their Table 1 cites Forster et al. (2007), i.e. AR4. The case-study factors use the EN 15804+A1 indicator set reported by LCAQuick 3.6 (CML characterisation); the underlying EPDs differ in IPCC GWP100 version (AR4 / AR5). The difference matters mainly for methane; A1–A5 is CO2-dominated, and the global side is bracketed by the EF 3.1 sensitivity.
- I_glob 5.58E+13 equals the EF 3.0 global factor (8.10E+03 kg CO₂e per person, 2010; Andreasi Bassi et al. 2023, Table 10), whose climate-change total sums the fossil, biogenic and land-use-change sub-indicators; the EF 3.1 value is a sensitivity (7.55E+03 kg CO₂e per person x 6,895,889,018 persons = 5.206E+13, 6.7% lower, mainly through the lower characterisation factor of methane in EF 3.1; acquired rights only).
- Ability-to-pay sector share: s_sec uses the consented value of new residential building over national final consumption expenditure, following the FCE upscaling of Hjalsted et al. (2021) as a proxy of the priority households give to housing. In the national accounts residential construction is gross fixed capital formation, not final consumption; treating it as consumed follows the endogenisation of capital in consumption-based accounting (Södersten, Wood & Hertwich 2018).
- Ability to pay: Hjalsted et al. (2021) state GDP as "USD/cap (2017)", World Bank (2019), without naming the series; current US$ is the sensitivity. The GDP coverage excludes economies without the measure (listed in outputs/data/aesa/results.json).
- Monte Carlo: I_sec,base is recomputed in every draw with that draw's case-study carbon factors (2025 technology) and on the 2016–2025 built floor area at that draw's completion rate (consents x completion rate; the census-measured net replacement behind the soil convention recomputed at that rate), so the factor and completion uncertainty are treated alike in the base and the projection (shared-parameter rule); the completion-rate and completion-lag one-at-a-time rows recompute the base from their own runs. It does not co-vary with the draw's dwelling size (the historical floor area is observed consents).
- The numerical results in Hjalsted et al.'s SI (Tables S4-S9) are reproduced only with α = 1; we apply α as specified in their Eq. 5 and SI Eq. S1, which ensures national shares sum to the global SOS. The authors have been contacted.

### Notes

- The manuscript world population 2025 (8,231,613,070) equals the WPP 2024 Median sheet x 1000; its 2026–2028 values differ from it by +/-0.5 person, consistent with a source at a higher precision than the 3-decimal thousands in this file; they are not a dating convention (the mean of 1 July t and t+1 differs by ~34 M).
- In the Monte Carlo the AR boundary varies with each draw's NZ population path and with I_sec,base recomputed from the draw's case-study carbon factors (2025 technology) on the observed history; the AtP boundary varies with population only. mc_base_fixed gives the bands with I_sec,base held at its deterministic value.

## 3. Pathways and the theoretical limit

### The lever rule

Ambition levels follow the 2050 Pathways Calculator (DECC 2010; DESNZ 2023) and EUCalc (D2.5, 2020): Reference = Level 1, Moderate = Level 2, Ambitious = Level 3, theoretical limit (TL) = Level 4. One rule for every lever (the 'rule' column): the Reference is current practice held (2023 / 2025 values; business-as-usual technology change applies in every run); Moderate is the midpoint of the Reference and Ambitious (exact for every lever); Ambitious is a documented frontier, achieved somewhere or projected by an authority, and cited; the theoretical limit is the logical bound where the lever has one (zero vacancy, zero space beyond the occupied area, no demolition, 100% brownfield, zero A4–A5), otherwise the best value observed (TL1 household size; the lowest-carbon NZ case study for materials). TL A4–A5 = 0 is a theoretical bound: construction waste cannot strictly reach zero, and LCAQuick does not split A4 from A5. Ambitious takes the first applicable sub-rule: A, a case-study distribution exists: the Harrell-Davis q0.15 quantile of the pooled scale-free case ratios (the top-15% convention of the EU Taxonomy, Delegated Regulation 2021/2139, Annex I s. 7.7), with a percentile bootstrap interval; B, an NZ record with no structural trend exists: the best value ever observed in NZ; C, otherwise: a published reference value (official projection > legislated target > peer-reviewed scenario > peer-country value). Moderate is the exact midpoint between the Reference and Ambitious in the lever's native parameter (per year for the path levers L1 and L9). TL is the definitional zero or full where one exists, else the best single observation, and is asserted at least as strong as Ambitious. Every level moves from the Reference along the normalised logistic 2026 -> 2035 (midpoint 2030.5, k = ln(81)/6), with two documented exceptions: L9 Ambitious and Moderate follow their own path (linear from the 2026 Reference value to zero in 2050, which is the phase-in itself); TL1 rises at the fastest observed inter-census change of household size (the behavioural speed limit) and reaches its level after 2035.

Levels between the Reference and Ambitious are indexed by lambda in [0, 1]: x(lambda) = x_ref + lambda (x_amb - x_ref), so Moderate is lambda = 0.5 exactly (tested for every lever); the lambda-sweep of each lever is in the Extended Data.

### The levers and the PAS 2080 strategies

The nine levers are grouped by the carbon reduction hierarchy of PAS 2080:2023 (BSI 2023, Clause 4.3 and Figure 5: Avoid - Switch - Improve). Classification rule: Avoid = levers that reduce the floor area needed to house the population, system level (number of dwellings) before asset level (floor area per dwelling); Switch = alternative site and materials for the floor area that is built (carbon per m²); Improve = construction efficiencies. Within a strategy the order follows the decision sequence (system before asset; site before materials). Avoid acts on floor area, Switch and Improve on carbon per m², the two axes of the solution space (Fig5).

#### S1 Avoid Strategies

**L1 Household size (sub-rule C).** S_Ambitious(t) = the Stats NZ propensity-B household size (Medium; living-arrangement propensities change, based on modelling of 2001–2023 Census data; Stats NZ DataInfo+, POPPR_FHH), rebased on the observed 2023 S exactly as the Reference propensity-A path, with the same post-2048 tail (end slope at 2048 = the 2043–2048 secant slope, continued linearly). Within one propensity the Stats NZ Low / Medium / High variants differ only through their population projections (age structure), so the earlier anchor (High - Medium) was not a behavioural change and is not used. In the pathway Monte Carlo each draw moves towards its own propensity-B path (Low / Medium / High B at the draw's population rank). B >= A in every year (asserted). The one-at-a-time row "Living arrangements: propensities change (Stats NZ B)" asks what happens if B happens anyway; L1 Ambitious asks what happens if policy delivers it. 2050: Reference 2.4635, Moderate 2.5275, Ambitious 2.5916. TL1: S = 2.7905, the highest observed national household size (1991), held regardless of age structure; with the 2050 population this requires about 11.7% fewer households per person than in 2023 at every age, living arrangements more shared than observed at any age. TL1 rises at the fastest observed inter-census change (0.0118 a year, 1996–2001), the behavioural speed limit, and reaches its level in 2037.5: the only TL whose phase-in ends after 2035.

**L2 Vacancy rate (sub-rule B).** Ambitious 4.01%, the 1996 census minimum on one definition (the pooled 2018/2023 empty share of unoccupied private dwellings applied to every census); Moderate (v_ref + v_min)/2 = 4.70%; TL2 v = 0. Reference = the published 2023 census value 5.39%; on the consistent definition 2023 is 5.38%.

**L3 Building lifetime (sub-rule C).** Demolition and the recent-surge component of net replacement x (1 - d), d = 0.40 (Pellan et al. 2024: 150,000 -> 90,000 demolitions a year), Moderate 0.20; TL3: zero demolition, no redevelopment wave; unconsented additions kept at the long-run rate. The census net replacement rates are context only.

**L4 Extra space (sub-rule B).** The Ambitious size is the smallest annual mean new-dwelling size ever consented, by typology, 1990–2025 (consented floor area / consents): Detached 148.8 m² (1990), Townhouses 105.8 m² (1990), Apartments 91.0 m² (1998). The Reference size is the 2023–2025 mean (Detached 187.6 m²), (Townhouses 108.0 m²), (Apartments 95.8 m²). The lever removes a share f of the extra-space margin (size - occupied area, occupied area = household size x OLF), f_t = (size_ref - size_min) / (size_ref - occ_ref), occ_ref = S_ref(2035) x OLF_t, so that the size at full strength equals the minimum; f_Ambitious = Detached 0.4117, Townhouses 0.0949, Apartments 0.1102; Moderate f/2; TL f = 1 (size = occupied area). It acts on the margin after L5. 1990 is the first year of the consent series and a recession year.

**L5 Occupancy density (sub-rule A).** For each of the 16 case studies (10 detached, 4 townhouses, 2 apartments; A_2 included as a distinct design) the design floor area per occupant (OLF) is divided by the median of its typology; r_Ambitious = HD q0.15 = 0.8194 (95% bootstrap interval 0.732–0.960, B = 2000); r_Moderate = (1 + r)/2 = 0.9097. The ratio scales every typology's OLF and dwelling size; TL5 per typology = min(own densest design ratio, r_Ambitious): Detached 0.7095, Townhouses 0.8194, Apartments 0.8194.

#### S2 Switch Strategies

**L6 Brownfield-first development (sub-rule C).** Share of new floor area on previously developed land: Ambitious 0.59 (England 2018–21, DLUHC 2022); Moderate (s_ref + 0.59)/2 = 0.339 with s_ref = 0.088 (the v3 Reference: replacement (soil-free) floor area / total, ratio of sums 2026–2050); TL6 s = 1. Context: US EPA (2014) infill share 21%. lambda = 0 is the lever off (the Reference); a constant s = s_ref would act in the years whose own replacement share is below s_ref. TL6 = 100% brownfield makes TL7 zero within TL.

**L7 Soil-aware planning (sub-rule C).** Soil carbon loss per m² x (1 - x), x = 0.146 (Christoforatos, Pickering & Schipper 2026), Moderate 0.073; TL7 the lowest soil order (Detached 22.9, Townhouses 13.8, Apartments 2.5 kg CO₂e/m²).

**L8 Material carbon efficiency (sub-rule A).** r = HD q0.15 of the 14 independent detached and townhouse case ratios A1-A3_i / pooled A1–A3 of the typology = 0.8270 (95% 0.607–0.950); Moderate (1 + r)/2 = 0.9135; TL8 Detached 0.530, Townhouses 0.827, Apartments 0.827 (detached: the best case, SD_2).

#### S3 Improve Strategy

**L9 Construction-stage carbon (sub-rule C).** Ambitious: A4–A5 from the 2026 Reference value linearly to zero by 2050 (Zero Carbon Act s. 5Q; City of Oslo 2025); Moderate: the per-year midpoint of the Reference path e^(-0.01 (t - 2025)) and Ambitious (2050 factor 0.389). L9 is phased once: Ambitious and Moderate follow their own path, which starts at the Reference in 2026, without the logistic adoption weight (MODEL v4.6 multiplied a path linear from 2025 by the logistic). TL9 A4–A5 = 0 is a theoretical bound (construction waste cannot strictly reach zero; LCAQuick does not split A4 from A5), adopted on the common logistic. A5 treated as energy: site waste assumed eliminated (upper bound).

### One run: payback and re-occupation

Every run follows the same order per year: gross_t -> overbuild payback -> re-occupation -> built_t. The 2026 overbuild of the Reference (the market excess) is computed once and held fixed in every run (the largest difference between runs is 0.0 dwellings); its absorption follows the Reference weights, the payback capped at max(gross_t, 0) with any shortfall carried. In the TL-family runs the dwellings released by TL1 (household decline) and TL2 (zero vacancy) to 2050, R = R1 + R2 (the overbuild is not in R), meet a constant share of each year's need after the payback, s = min(R, G+)/G+, G+ = sum over 2027–2050 of max(gross_t, 0); the cumulative re-occupied never exceeds the cumulative released: where that binds the shortfall is built and s is recomputed from the remaining pool; R > G+ leaves a surplus vacant in 2050. Re-occupied dwellings are attributed to TL1 and TL2 in proportion R1 : R2.

TL: R1 = 0, R2 = 117,834, G+ = 315,033, s = 0.542; the release constraint binds in no year; need is non-positive (nothing built) in no year; surplus vacant 2050 0. Instant TL (sensitivity): R1 = 78,964, R2 = 115,360, s = 0.677.

## 4. Attribution principle, release accounting, replacement and the history

#### Attribution principle and system boundary

Emissions fully determined at construction (A1–A5, soil carbon loss) are attributed to the construction year; emissions depending on later decisions or technology (B, C1–C4) are time-resolved (in-window counted, remainder committed). System boundary: new residential construction, identical for the AR/AtP base (2016–2025) and the projection (2026–2050). Demand uses the existing stock (vacancy, overbuild absorption, re-occupation, replacement); emissions of the existing stock are outside scope on both sides. The committed emissions of an investment decision are attributed to the decision (Davis & Socolow 2014, Environ. Res. Lett. 9, 084018).

#### Release accounting (bands.py; pathways.run)

Positive demand bands are always gross need: population growth, smaller households, extra space, vacancy (the gross allowance: on new households and any vacancy-rate rise), the 2026 overbuild, demolition replacement and the recent replacement surge. Every release is its own negative band, booked in the year it is used: 'Overbuild absorbed' (the payback, taken on the gross need), 'Unconsented additions' (the calibrated residual of the census identity), 'Vacancy released' (a vacancy-rate fall in a run without any lever at its theoretical limit: used in the year it occurs, capped at that year's gross need, the rest carried forward) and 'Released dwellings (TL)' (the re-occupation pool). No release is netted inside a positive band and no band is rescaled: retirement-village units are a constant share of every dwelling built, so each in-scope band is its gross floor area times (1 - that share), exactly. If gross need minus usable releases is negative in a year, nothing is built and the unusable amount is carried forward against the next years: released dwellings remain available later, as they do in the theoretical-limit re-occupation pool. Whatever is still unusable in 2050 is booked in 2050 against its release band and as 'Surplus kept vacant (2050)', so the bands add up to the total in every year (checked to 1e-9). In every theoretical-limit-family run (TL, the TL steps of both waterfalls, every TL Shapley subset) the re-occupation pool holds every dwelling release present in the run (a vacancy-rate fall at any level, a household-size fall), with the constant-share rule, the availability constraint and attribution in proportion to the release of each source.

#### Zero-year guard (engine.forward)

A year whose built floor area is below 1e-06 m² is a year in which nothing is built: its floor area, soil-bearing share and soil carbon are set to 0. The soil-bearing share is clipped to [0, 1] in every run. Without the guard the share 1 - soil-free / total is a ratio of floating-point noise and the soil carbon of a year without construction is non-zero (seen in pathway Monte Carlo draws; no deterministic run is affected).

#### History by census interval (validation.history_bands)

The residual band of the history is split into the census-measured net replacement (the interval rate of the census dwelling-count identity x the previous year's stock x the year's dwelling size; it may be negative, e.g. 1996–2001), the retirement-village units (negative, out of scope) and the unexplained building (the remainder to the observed in-scope floor area built; it may be negative, e.g. 2013–2018). The bands add up to the observed floor area built in every interval (checked to 1e-9). Over 1992–2025 the unexplained building sums to 3,215 dwellings (+0.40% of the 803,534 built); the floor-area remainder equals the unexplained dwellings of the stock identity x the dwelling size (difference 5.1e-15 Mm²).

#### Replacement in the Reference and its variants

Net replacement fades from the 2018–23 census rate (0.17%) to the long-run 1991–2023 rate (0.06%), half-life 10 yr; BRANZ demolition (0.135%) only splits the net rate into the demolition, surge and unconsented-additions bands. The half-life is not identifiable from the census record (seven censuses, six interval rates), so the Monte Carlo samples it, U(5, 15) yr, with the deterministic 10 yr as its median (it acts in the Reference variant only). The functional form matters little for the cumulative surge: the mean excess over the long-run rate 2026–2050 is 0.052 pp with the 10-yr half-life and 0.055 pp for a linear path that reaches the long-run rate in 2050.

Very High replacement (trend continues; a sensitivity variant): the 6 census-interval rates 1991–2023 fitted by weighted least squares on the mean of each interval's years (weights = interval length), rate = -0.121385 + 6.0725e-05 x year, extrapolated 2026–2050: 0.164% in 2026 and 0.310% in 2050. It is not adopted as the Reference: 6 interval rates (7 censuses), 2 of them negative (1996–2001, 2001–2006), the 2013–2018 census definition break (empty / residents-away dwellings), and the unbounded extrapolation of a policy-driven wave.

#### Completion rate in the Monte Carlo

Uniform on [0.93, 0.96]. The bounds are published completion milestones for Auckland consents (Greenaway-McGrevy & Jones 2023; Jones, Greenaway-McGrevy & Crow 2025, Policy Quarterly 21(1), 63–68, p. 68 and footnote 12): 93% of 2018–2019 consents had a final inspection by July 2024 (lower bound of eventual completion) and more than 95% of 2018–2021 consents had a first inspection (upper bound; the article gives no point value, so the edge 0.96 is a stated judgement). The deterministic central value 0.945 is their midpoint, and so the median of the Monte Carlo input. No shape inside the band is identified, hence uniform. Limitation: Auckland evidence applied nationally.

#### Consent-to-completion lag and pipeline years

Completions in month m = 0.945 x consents in month m - L, L = 17 months, aggregated to calendar years. L is the midpoint of the median time to dwelling completion of 1.27–1.53 yr for Auckland consents as of July 2024 (Greenaway-McGrevy & Jones 2023; Jones, Greenaway-McGrevy & Crow 2025), consistent with the Stats NZ Experimental building indicators (dwelling-weighted median 455 days from consent to final inspection for December 2020 quarter consents, 533 days for September 2022 quarter consents). The same lag applies everywhere consents become dwellings: the stock identity, the census-interval net replacement rates (consents lagged L/12 years before each census date), the dwelling-size and typology-mix windows, historical floor area and the AR / AtP base, and the projection start. Projection years whose twelve lagged months are all observed (2026, 2027) are pipeline years: their building is observed in every run (the market excess over the requirement), and the excess fades from the next year at the persistence rho re-estimated on the lagged history. Before April 1990 the typology columns of the consent file are empty; those months are split by the April 1990 - March 1991 typology ratios of all dwellings (they enter only the 1991 completions, which are used in the cumulative floor area from 1991 and nowhere else). Limitations: one fixed lag (no distribution of build times), Auckland evidence applied nationally. The rolling-origin hindcast of the census dwelling-count identity is not worse at L = 17 than at L = 0 (outputs/data/baseline/completion_lag_hindcast.csv).

#### Theoretical limit: constraints at Level 4

Level 4 is the definitional limit of each lever, reached along the common adoption window, except household size (TL1): its level (2.7905, the 1991 census maximum) is approached no faster than the fastest change of household size observed between consecutive censuses 1991–2023 (0.01176 per year, 1996–2001; census-benchmarked households): S_TL(t) = min(S_ref(2026) + r (t - 2026), level), never below the Ambitious path. The level is reached in 2037.5. Household size is a population-level outcome of age structure, partnering and housing costs; the speed limit keeps the theoretical limit within changes the New Zealand census record has shown. The instant-TL row keeps its definition (every level from 2027). In every theoretical-limit-family run the Reference's overbuild surplus (the positive market excess of the pipeline years and of the fading gap) enters the re-occupation pool with the TL1 / TL2 releases (constant share of each year's positive need, availability constraint, carry-forward); the re-occupied overbuild is booked in 'Overbuild absorbed'. Releases of an observed (pipeline) year enter the pool in the first unobserved year.

#### Household-size projection

Household size follows the Stats NZ 2023-base national family and household projections (POPPR_FHH_008 people in households over POPPR_FHH_010 households, five-yearly 2023–2048; DataInfo+ https://datainfoplus.stats.govt.nz/item/nz.govt.stats/e7475c01-9e55-491d-a8fe-74efa8fba757), Medium A (living-arrangement propensities held at 2023), as a shape rebased on the observed 2023 household size of the census households and the total population; this holds the share of the population outside private dwellings at its 2023 level. The 5th / 95th population paths take the Low A / High A projections (within one propensity the projections differ only through their population projections; the Monte Carlo pairs them through one z). Sensitivities: Medium B (propensities change, modelled on the 2001–2023 censuses) and the 2018–2023 census pace continued linearly from 2023, for the Reference, the Moderate / Ambitious Pathway and TL (sensitivity/household_size.csv). Extra space grows with smaller households: its floor area is new households x (dwelling size - occupied area per dwelling), and a smaller household size means more new households for the same population and a smaller occupied area per dwelling.

#### Check and sensitivity rows

TL with re-occupation as fast as demand allows (deterministic sensitivity row): 3,550.7 kt, LoE AR 0.802 (TL: 4,079.1 kt, LoE AR 0.921).

TL1 age-standardised (deterministic sensitivity row): TL1 at the household size given by the lower of the 2023 and Stats NZ Medium B living-arrangement (headship) rates by age group (0–14, 15–39, 40–64, 65+; POPPR_FHH_008 / POPPR_FHH_010), applied to the projected population (household_headship.py; the 2023 rates are the only observed ones by age in the repository, so the highest observed propensity of living with others is the 2023 one; the 2023-rate path reproduces the Stats NZ Medium A household size to within 0.022). Its 2050 level is 2.5669 against the L1 Ambitious 2.5916; below the L1 Ambitious path in 2040–2050, where the TL rule (never weaker than Ambitious) holds TL1 at Ambitious (the age-standardised level itself in 2026–2039): TL 5,946.4 kt, LoE AR 1.343, LoE AtP 5.34 (TL: 4,079.1 kt, LoE AR 0.921). In the pathway Monte Carlo (each draw's own household size and population variant) P(LoE AR <= 1) = 0.1% (TL: 64.0%).

L8 with the apartment case A_1 (n = 15): r = 0.841 against the adopted 0.827 (n = 14); report only (A_1's ratio to its pooled value is 1.0000 by construction).

## 5. Uncertainty analysis

Joint uncertainty is propagated by Latin hypercube sampling (McKay, Beckman & Conover 1979): 5,000 draws in the full profile (seed 20260924) and 1,000 in the light profile (seed 20261014) of the 5 inputs below, for the Reference only (replacement-level uncertainty is reported by the variants of ED3 and the one-at-a-time rows). The reported results are those of the full profile (5,000 draws in montecarlo/draws_REF.csv). Each draw runs the same forward functions as the deterministic projection (engine.py), which uses the median of every sampled input; the central draw is checked against the projection to 1e-9.

| input | distribution | basis | 5th / 50th / 95th percentile of the draws |
|---|---|---|---|
| z_pop (population and household size) | standard normal; one rank in every year (comonotone) | Stats NZ 2024-base stochastic population projection: the published level spread at the 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 95th percentiles, linear in z; household size by the same z through the Stats NZ 2023-base Low / Medium / High A household projections placed at z = -1.645 / 0 / 1.645 | -1.64 / 0.00 / 1.64 |
| size (dwelling size) | lognormal multiplier, σ = 0.0634 | RMS log deviation of annual typology dwelling sizes 2016–2025 from the adopted reference | 0.901 / 1.000 / 1.110 |
| complete (completion rate) | uniform(0.93, 0.96) | completion milestones of Auckland consents (Greenaway-McGrevy & Jones 2023; Jones, Greenaway-McGrevy & Crow 2025); the stock calibration, the census replacement rates, the 2024–2025 starting surplus and the acquired-rights base are redone in each draw | 0.931 / 0.945 / 0.959 |
| carbon (case-study carbon factors) | uniform index into 4,000 bootstrap replicates | stratified bootstrap of the case studies within sub-type (duplicates removed, re-pooled as Building_factors); the apartments (one independent case) take a mean-preserving lognormal multiplier with the pooled between-building log-SD of the other sub-types | 0.05 / 0.50 / 0.95 |
| half_life (replacement half-life) | uniform(5, 15) yr | not identifiable from the census record; the Reference variant only | 5.5 / 10.0 / 14.5 |

Population and household size share one draw because, within one living-arrangement propensity, the Stats NZ 2023-base Low / Medium / High household projections differ only through their population projections (the 5th / 50th / 95th percentiles of the stochastic population projection), so the household size moves with the population percentile (N4, resolved). Not sampled: the living-arrangement propensity (A, held at 2023; B, the change modelled on the 2001–2023 censuses, is a one-at-a-time row), the net replacement level (the Reference only; its half-life is sampled; the variants are reported deterministically in ED3 and the one-at-a-time rows), the typology mix, the census rebase of households, the pre-2013 empty share, the future vacancy and the retirement-village share (total Sobol indices about zero in a full-input run), the demolition rate (it trades one-for-one with the calibrated residual), the observed consents and population (data) and the soil order (a bounding scenario, not a probability).

In every draw the acquired-rights base Ī_sec,base is recomputed from that draw's carbon-factor replicate on the 2016–2025 built floor area at that draw's completion rate (boundaries.mc_runs, boundaries.history_at_completion, boundaries.base_with_factors): the carbon factors and the completion rate are shared parameters of the base and the projection and are sampled once (the shared-parameter rule of Part 2). Each draw also recomputes the 2024–2025 stock-identity residual and its starting surplus at its own completion rate. Ī_sec,base over the draws: 1,330.9 / 1,413.4 / 1,501.3 kt/yr (5th / 50th / 95th percentile).

**Variance-based sensitivity.** First-order and total Sobol indices of the Reference (full profile): base sample N = 1,024 (7,168 model evaluations), the estimators of Saltelli et al. (2010) and Jansen (1999) as implemented in scipy.stats.sobol_indices (scipy 1.17.1), with BCa 95% intervals from 999 bootstrap resamples (Efron 1987). Total indices of cumulative carbon 2026–2050: Population and household size 0.64 (0.59–0.69), Dwelling size 0.26 (0.23–0.28), Carbon factors 0.10 (0.09–0.11). Population and household size are one grouped input (one z, perfectly dependent): their indices are grouped Sobol indices (Jacques, Lavergne & Devictor 2006).

**Pathway Monte Carlo** (pathways_mc.py). The Reference, the Moderate and Ambitious Pathways and the Theoretical Limit are run on the same draws (paired), so their differences are draw by draw. The importance of each input for floor area, carbon and the cumulative LoE of AR is given by standardised regression coefficients and partial rank correlation coefficients (Marino et al. 2008) with percentile bootstrap intervals (2,000 resamples).

**Committed after 2050.** For every Reference draw the committed emissions (the later B2/B4 events of the 2026–2050 cohorts and their C1–C4) are computed with pathways.committed on that draw's floor area by typology; the repair and end-of-life factors are held at their central values, so the range comes from the floor-area uncertainty (population, household size, dwelling size, completion rate). At the lower decarbonisation bound (2050 factors held for the later events): central 9,728 kt, median 9,726 kt, 50% interval 9,069–10,456, 90% interval 8,160–11,519 kt (pathways/montecarlo_summary.csv; per draw in pathways/montecarlo_draws.csv).

The share of draws in which TL stays within the AR budget is 64.0% (3,200 of 5,000; Wilson 95% interval 62.7–65.3%, Wilson 1927). The 2050 population at which P(TL LoE AR ≤ 1) = 50% is 6.72 million (95% interval 6.71–6.72), from a univariate logistic regression on the draw's 2050 population fitted by Firth's penalised likelihood where the maximum-likelihood estimate does not exist (Firth 1993; Heinze & Schemper 2002), with a percentile bootstrap of 2,000 resamples (seed 20263025 in the full profile).
